Twenty art-directed faces rendered by the shipped AGSL fragment shaders, over the theme's own field, with the canonical theme audit run against the app's palettes. The previous renders were a Python silk field that the app does not draw; these are the shader the app actually runs.

The rendered set

Nine families (plus the app's own default pair), light and dark adjacent, in the same order every time. 390×844, rendered at 2×.

Each card is the ground plane of one face: the field ramp, its three colour pools, the plate, and the ambient film. The swatch strip below each pair is the face's authored vocabulary — light then dark, for the same role.

Home, all twenty faces

The same maths at page scale. The ground plane is the WebGL canvas; every pane of glass on top of it — the crown, the hero, the goal card, the navigation capsule — is drawn by LIQUID_GLASS_AGSL, run once per surface shape and composited by the page source-over, which is what Skia does with the premultiplied half4 it returns. That shader never samples the backdrop, and that is the property that makes this affordable rather than a second renderer.

What each layer is drawn by

  • the field — folioField: the ramp along the pack's own light axis, plus three colour pools at poolAlpha 0.09 dark / 0.08 light.
  • the plate — GUILLOCHE_AGSL, on the app's single ground plane, with its figure derived from the pack id.
  • the ambient film — AMBIENT_AGSL, a second full-screen pass, blended ONE / ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA because it returns premultiplied.
  • every pane of glass — LIQUID_GLASS_AGSL. Its fill alpha is the model's, not a designer's: the crown uses topBarFill, the capsule navCapsuleFill (0.60 with blur), the card panelFill, the hero the atmosphere's paneAlpha.
  • the layout — FolioTokens: the 20dp gutter, the 56dp bar, the 148/84dp cover ladder at aspect 1.5, and the shape family's radii — the hero's 34 / 20 / 34 / 8, the card's 18, the capsule's pill.

The AGSL output, measured

Everything above audits the source hexes. That answers "is the palette well designed?" and not "did the shader preserve it?". So each face is also rendered twice — once with the AGSL passes, once without — over a grid of role patches, and the patches are sampled. Splitting the pipeline is what makes a failure attributable:

source  →  A (compositing)  →  plain (the app's alpha)  →  full (F_AGSL)

Left pair: Lagoon, with and without the AGSL passes. Right pair: Dusk. Row A is each role as a flat fill — it reproduces the source hexes exactly. Row B/C is the same role through the stack the app gives it.

The shader is a renderer, not a palette generator

The four accent roles come out of the shader at ΔE 0.00 on every face — they are opaque fills and the shader never touches them. The substrate moves by at most 2.26 ΔE and the glass panes by at most 2.26. So the answer to the question that matters is yes: the shader preserves the validated relationships rather than re-authoring them.

One honest qualification. The substrate's hue does drift, by up to 4.4° on six role/face pairs (against a 3° bound) — all of them on the page plane at Oklab chroma below 0.02, where a hue angle is close to meaningless and the corresponding ΔE is under 2.3. I am reporting the six rather than moving the bound to make them go away, but I would not treat them as defects.

The crown measurement contradicts the curation note — and I think the note is about a different crown

The curation record says the fitted accentProgress cleared the wordmark contrast on all eighteen faces where raw display colours did not. Measured on the rendered crown, the opposite holds: textPrimary — the app's actual choice — clears 4.2:1 on 20 / 20, while accentProgress clears on only 12 / 20, worst at jade-light 3.12 and terracotta-light 3.18.

The likely reason is that the two are not measuring the same surface. The spec's §5 describes a crown that is a darkened brand-coloured strip — "on paper it is darkened strongly (roughly 0.12–0.48 toward the ink)". The app's crown is topBarFill: the page colour at 0.35 alpha, so on paper it is a pale band (0xDED4CC on Lagoon), and a pale band wants dark ink. On that surface the note's conclusion does not transfer, and the app's current choice is the right one.

Either way it is worth your eye: if you intend the crown to be the darkened strip the spec describes, then the contrast question re-opens and the answer may well flip back.

What the in-app crown says

The wordmark really is textPrimary. The glyph sampled out of the title region matches the palette's textPrimary at ΔE 1.7–3.8 on all seven captures — so the app draws colors.onSurface, and that is confirmed by measurement rather than by reading the call site.

In-app contrast is 13.3–17.4:1, far above the 4.2 floor. On the dark faces both candidates clear comfortably, so the dark row does not discriminate between them. The discriminating cases are the light faces, and there is no light-face device capture in the repository — so the light-face result below rests on the reconstruction.

Correcting something I said last turn

I claimed the reconstruction's crown used the wrong alpha tier — 0.35, the unblurred path, where a real device takes glassTierAlpha(0.35, 0.35, 0.25) = 0.25 — and that "every contrast number taken against it was taken against the wrong surface". The first half is true and now fixed. The second half is overstated: because the fill colour is the page, the two tiers composite to within 1.34 ΔE worst case across all twenty faces. It does not explain the gap.

The gap is real but small: on Dusk, the reconstruction's crown ground is 0x120D1D against the device's 0x1E0D22, ΔE 2.9. That residual is not the alpha tier and is most likely the device build — the capture predates the current source — plus the device's own colour management. I have not attributed it further, and I would not read anything into a 2.9 ΔE from a screenshot of unknown build.

Against the spec's §5

§5 asks for the crown to be "the strongest brand-colored structural strip", "a gradient band", and on paper "darkened strongly (roughly 0.12–0.48 toward the ink)". The app's crown is topBarFill: the page colour at 0.25 alpha, plus a scrim under the status icons, a specular sheen along the daylight axis, and a hairline at its foot. On paper that is a pale band — 0xDED4CC on Lagoon, 0xD7DBD2 on Dawn — not a darkened brand strip.

So the two are different surfaces, and the contrast question resolves differently on each: a pale band wants dark ink, which is what the app uses and why it clears 20 / 20. Measured on the rendered crown, accentProgress clears only 12 / 20 — worst at jade-light 3.12, terracotta-light 3.18, moonstone-light 3.34. If the crown is ever changed to the darkened strip §5 describes, that answer should be re-measured rather than assumed to flip or to hold.

The reconstruction now carries the sheen and the hairline, which it did not before, so the crown it draws is at least the right shape even where it is not the right pixels.

The chrome / frame contract

The images now show the app's actual crown

Earlier versions of this section drew a chromeAccent role this pipeline had invented, which is not what the app does. They have been re-rendered: the crown is now atmosphere.barGlass — the chrome plane, not the page — at topBarFill(1, blurred)'s own alphas, with the three-stop veil, the three-stop status scrim, the rim-light sheen, the foot fade and the hairline. The capsule is navigationSurface at navCapsuleFill(true) = 0.60, and its selected pill wears the destination's accent (progress for Home, streak for Stats) rather than the palette's single signature.

So the re-render sits 3.8 ΔE from the device where the proposal sat 14.5. The residual is the remaining structural gap: the sheen is a CSS gradient at a computed angle rather than a drawRect along daylightGradient(...), the scrim's mid stop is approximated, and the capture predates the current source.

The clause analysis below is still a proposal evaluation, not a measurement of these images. It asks what would happen if the crown were re-derived from the accent vocabulary, and it is computed analytically from the derived roles. Read it as a design proposal with its own arithmetic, alongside a render of what ships.

The diagnosis is that the crown and the navigation were inheriting the surface family — topBarFill is a page treatment — so both edges of the UI collapsed toward the substrate instead of framing it. So the chrome here is not derived from backgroundBase at all. It is placed at an accent's hue and its lightness and chroma are solved to land inside the contract's salience band with as much chroma as the gamut holds there.

place at the accent's hue → sweep lightness → keep the most chroma inside CS ∈ band and above CL ≥ floor

What the derivation delivers outright

c3 accent ownership: 9/9. The chrome is placed at an accent's hue by construction, so it is always within 40° of the vocabulary — that clause is satisfied by the method rather than by luck.

c8 and c9, both text clauses: 9/9. chromeOnFill is chosen from {textPrimary, white, black} by the actual rendered fill, and clears 4.5:1 at 10.5–18.6:1; navOnActive at 12.0–16.7:1. Fitting the on-colour to the fill works.

Two clauses are provably incompatible with clause 1 — not merely failing

c5 (dominance rank) cannot hold while c1 (salience ceiling) does. Clause 1 caps the crown at 0.18–0.20 from the page. The roles it must outrank sit at 0.25–0.70. A value at most 0.20 cannot outrank a value of 0.40, so no placement satisfies both. Measured: the crown ranks 14–18 of 20 over the full UI pool.

I then re-ran the rank over the reading the contract's own sentence supports — "buried beneath tertiary UI colours" — restricting the pool to the quiet frame roles (text ladder, borders, guilloche, glows, progress track). It still fails, at 7–11 of 12, because those roles are placed at extreme lightness against the page and so sit 0.25+ away. The clause needs a pool definition that excludes them, or clause 1 needs a different shape.

c6 (cross-mode lift) cannot hold while c1 does either. It requires CL_dark ≥ CL_light. Every light page here is a near-neutral cream (C 0.004–0.027) while the dark pages carry more (C 0.006–0.041), so for the same absolute chrome chroma the light face gets the bigger lift. On Lagoon the light crown lifts 0.091 against the dark's 0.076 — and to match it the dark crown would need C 0.113, which sits beyond the 0.20 salience cap. The requirement systematically favours whichever mode has the more neutral substrate, which on this palette set is light.

Both failures are therefore findings about the contract, not about the palettes. The shape I would try: make clause 1 a floor with a chroma ceiling instead of a ΔE ceiling, and let c5 and c6 follow.

And one clause pair that conflicts only sometimes

c3 and c7 pull against each other. c3 says derive the chrome from the accent vocabulary; c7 says the chrome must stay inside the family's semantic anchor band. Those agree only when the primary accent is the anchor hue. On Lagoon the anchor is teal (150–210°) but primaryAccent is coral (33°), so a crown derived from the primary lands 117° outside the anchor. Same on Arctic, Jade and Moonstone. c4 also fails on Arctic and Nebula, where the chosen counterpoint sits inside 25° of the crown.

10 of 18 inside the budget. The light faces cluster at 0.119–0.126 — just over — because the crown band is the full 100dp status-plus-bar strip and the capsule is a wide pill, and an opaque chromatic fill over both is 12–13% of a 390×844 viewport on its own. More interesting: on Forest, Terracotta, Jade and Arctic dark the hot-pixel count is 0.0008–0.0012, because the derived dark crown's chroma (0.047–0.074) is below clause 10's own 0.08 threshold. So by the contract's own definition of "high-chroma", those dark crowns are not visibly coloured — they are only lifted. That is clause 1's ceiling showing up a second time, from a different direction.

Implementing it exposed a real bug in the reconstruction

The crown markup never included the status-bar spacer, so the element was 56dp where it should have been 100dp and the 44dp above main showed the bare page. With a page-coloured crown that was completely invisible — the crown and the page were the same colour. Making the crown chromatic revealed it immediately. It is fixed, and it is a small argument for the contract's own thesis: a surface-coloured frame hides its own defects.

Target reached: the plane placed at the measured optimum

L 0.65 for both modes, and the picture changes completely

The sweep said every face reaches its target at L ≈ 0.65, so both planes were moved there (the light one from 0.70, the dark one from 0.28) with the chroma cap raised to 0.16 and the material share to 0.90.

The dark row was the whole problem and it is now solved — dark GCC went from 0.027 to 0.10, and dark VS from 0.032 to 0.12, both comfortably past their floors. That was a placement error, exactly as the ceiling sweep said, and it is fixed in the app.

1 / 18 passes every floor (Dawn dark). The remaining gap is narrow and one-sided: light VS.

A vertical profile of the bar explains it. topBarFill decays the veil down the bar — 0.42 at the crown, 0.218 at 60%, 0.080 at the foot — so the crown's salience peaks near its top and again at its foot, and sags in the decayed middle:

position on the barveil alphaVSfloor
35% down0.350.07500.08
50% down0.320.06800.08
72% down0.180.04920.08
92% down0.110.07940.08

So the light floor of 0.08 is short everywhere on the bar, not only in the sampled region — the best point reaches 0.0794 against 0.08, a 1% miss, and the sampled middle sits at 0.049–0.061. Dropping the light plane from 0.65 to 0.58 lifted light VS from 0.045–0.053 to 0.054–0.061 and light GCC to 0.128–0.163, without moving light VC.

The remaining 1% is not worth another round: it is below the reproducibility of a screenshot comparison, and the honest reading is that a near-white page plus a 0.42 alpha ceiling puts the light floor fractionally out of reach.

Why light VS is the last holdout

VS is a full ΔE, so it carries the lightness difference as well as the chroma. On paper the page is already near-white, so a plane at L 0.65 composited at 0.42 moves the body only to L ≈ 0.83 — a modest lightness step, and the chroma contributes the rest. Dark has the opposite geometry: a near-black page against the same plane gives a much larger ΔL, which is why dark VS clears 0.10 while light sits at 0.05.

So the light floor of 0.08 is measuring something the light substrate cannot supply at this placement, for the same reason the earlier gamut sweep kept finding: a near-white page has nowhere to go. The lever, if the floor must hold, is a darker plane on light faces — which is a design call rather than a constant, and I have not made it.

Is the dark floor reachable? Yes — at a different lightness

The ceiling is 0.10, and every face can reach its target — at L ≈ 0.65

Before tuning further I computed the hard bound rather than guessing at it. The chain is short: VC_body = alpha · (C_plane − C_page), with alpha capped at 0.42 by the §15 glass window and C_plane capped by the gamut at the plane's lightness. Sweeping every lightness at the legal alpha gives the ceiling:

faceC_pageVC at the page's lightnessVC ceilingtarget
ocean dark0.02200.00480.10060.040
nebula dark0.0412−0.00170.09250.040
jade dark0.00570.01140.10740.040
ocean light0.01240.00420.10460.025

10 / 10 light and 10 / 10 dark faces can reach their target at some plane lightness — and every single one of them needs L ≈ 0.65. The ceiling is 2.5× the dark target, so this was never a gamut wall. It is a placement problem.

That is the whole explanation of the remaining gap. The light plane is placed at L 0.70, close to 0.65, and light VC now measures 0.015–0.025 — essentially at target. The dark plane is placed at L 0.28, and at that lightness the gamut holds so little chroma that the body can only reach 0.0048–0.0114.

So the two instructions conflict, and it needs your call

The earlier brief specified "DARK: L(barGlass) ≈ 0.16–0.32". The VC target needs L ≈ 0.65. Both cannot hold, and the arithmetic is not close.

Moving the dark plane to 0.65 would make the dark crown a mid-tone band on a near-black page — composite lightness ~0.32 against a page at 0.085. That is genuinely "coloured glass", and it is a visible character change: the crown becomes a lit strip rather than a dark one. It is a design decision, not a tuning constant, so I have not made it unilaterally.

Three options, all one-line changes now that the arithmetic is known:

  • Move the dark plane to L 0.65. Hits the target. The dark crown becomes a lit chromatic band.
  • Keep L 0.28 and accept a lower dark floor (~0.012). The dark crown stays dark and the contract's dark target is documented as above what that placement permits.
  • Split the difference — L 0.45, say — for a partially lit crown reaching roughly 0.06.

Raising the three glass structures

The layer attribution cleared the suspects

Before touching anything I attributed the crown body's chroma to each layer in turn — veil alone, then +scrim, then +sheen. Every column came out identical: the overlays remove 0%. My scrim/sheen hypothesis was simply wrong; at the body's sample point neither layer is even present. The limiter is the pane's own α = 0.25 and nothing else.

That is worth stating plainly because the previous section speculated the opposite, and the measurement took one script to settle it.

What was raised, in the app

surfacechangewhy this is legal
mastheadBAR_GLASS_BLURRED 0.25 → 0.42the §15 glass window is 0.22–0.42; 0.42 is its ceiling, not a new regime
cardsCARD_GLASS_CHROMA 0.06 → 0.10, CARD_MATERIAL_SHARE 0.55 → 0.80gamut-safe throughout — the chroma is still clamped to maxChromaInGamut
nav pill0.45 → 0.60the contract's own band is 0.40–0.65

The renderer was lying — three times

You were right: the crown was not drawn the way the app draws it

The screenshot showed a crown the same colour as the page with only a coloured edge. That was the render, not the app. Tracing the app's chain against the renderer's turned up three separate divergences, each of which made the render understate the crown while the report claimed to describe the app.

#the app doesthe renderer did
1 barGlass → barGlassFor applies tintGlass → FolioTopBar composites at topBarFill's alphas composited barGlass directly — skipped the tint pass, so it drew a less chromatic plane than ships
2 the hero pane is folioRaised: atmos.raisedFill at paneAlpha filled raw surface — never read raisedFill at all, so the card material change was invisible here
3 one material model, consumed by the composables a second implementation in Python that recomputed the card material and read none of the controls

All three are fixed. The crown body on Ember now measures (22,10,15) against a page of (11,8,12) — a visibly warm band, not a page-coloured one.

And the check that caught the third one

The brief's integrity clause, implemented as integrity.py: render each surface with its control on and off and measure the pixel difference. A control that changes state but not pixels is a failed control, whatever the state says.

controlgovernsΔE on/offverdict
bar glassthe crown's veil0.013 – 0.125connected
crown corethe 5dp band0.100 – 0.424connected
card materialthe hero pane's fill0.003 – 0.014 connected (was 0.00000 — dead — until divergences 2 and 3 were fixed)
glass tintthe barGlassFor pass 0.0008 – 0.010 connected, but ~0.001 on light faces

The first run reported 11 dead controls, all with a difference of exactly 0.00000. That number is what a disconnected control looks like, and it is the reason the clause exists: without it, the card material would have been reported as measured when nothing had been measured.

The last row is worth its own note. The tintGlass pass is connected, but on light faces its contribution is ~0.001 ΔE — below perceptibility. A pass that costs a full colour transform and changes nothing visible is a candidate for removal, not for tuning.

Applied to the app

What landed in the Kotlin

These are no longer only proposals. Six files changed, and :shared:compileKotlinDesktop reports BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 0 errors.

filechange
theme/FolioAtmosphere.kt a chromeAccent role; tintGlass() with the GLASS_TINT_* / GLASS_CHROMA_BOOST_* / GLASS_LIGHTNESS_SHARE_* constants; oklabL(); fillForm() + FILL_ACCENT_CHROMA
theme/FolioFieldModel.kt barGlassFor tints the pane before the book tint, so the untinted branch is tinted too — the book is not what makes the bar a bar
theme/Theme.kt FolioTokens.chromeCoreHeight = 5.dp, chromeCoreAlpha = 0.62f
components/FolioChrome.kt the chromatic core: a 5dp band at the bar's foot, horizontal gradient 0.62 → 0.26, drawn under the foot fade
nav/FolioNavShell.kt the pill takes fillForm(accent) at alpha 0.45
theme/FolioAtmosphere.kt (this pass) chromeGlassMaterial() + mixOklab(); barGlass is now mixOklab(barGlassBase, chromeGlassMaterial(chromeAccent, dark), 0.80) — a placed plane, not a mix of two near-neutral inputs. Plus cardGlassMaterial() applied to raisedFill and panelFill, so the cards carry the same chrome hue at their own lightness

Card material. folioRaised reads atmos.raisedFill (FolioSurfaces.kt:183), so the cards now speak the same material language as the bar — same hue, their own lightness and mixing share. The gamut at a card's lightness holds only ~0.01–0.05 chroma, so on paper this is a hue contribution and at night a genuinely chromatic one. The bar stays the stronger of the two; the hierarchy is page → bar → card.

fillForm had to be public: internal is not visible across Gradle modules, and FolioNavShell lives in androidApp.

I did not wire navigationSelected into the pill — the source forbids it, and it is right to

Theme.kt says of that role: "Authored on all 18 art-directed faces, and deliberately NOT read by the nav capsule — do not 'fix' this by wiring it into the selected pill." The reason is substantive: one fixed colour for all four tabs flattens the per-room differentiation the capsule builds on purpose.

But the rendered-output measurement found something the source-side audit could not: the destination accents are AA-fitted for ink, and a role fitted as foreground text is the wrong value for a fill. So I measured three options rather than swapping one for the other:

nav active fillpasses the visible floors
the destination accent as authored (ink-fitted)6 / 18
the destination accent's fill form — same hue, more chroma 18 / 18
navigationSelected (the forbidden one)18 / 18

The fill form matches the forbidden option on salience while keeping the destination hue, so the differentiation the source protects survives and the single-table contract with the masthead's segment switch is untouched. Only the role's fitting changes, from ink to fill.

Alpha swept against the floors: 0.20 → 0/18, 0.35 → 15/18, 0.40 → 16/18, 0.45 → 18/18. 0.45 is the measured minimum, not a taste.

The contract's VC_glass floor is unreachable — and that is a finding about the contract

Clause 4 asks the glass body for a visible chroma lift of 0.025 (light) / 0.040 (dark). Measured, with the tint already at the contract's maximum (τ 0.18 light / 0.30 dark, k 1.25 / 1.45), the body delivers 0.002–0.014 — and sweeping the pane's alpha does not rescue it:

pane alphaworst VC, lightworst VC, darkfloor
0.25 (as designed)−0.0043−0.00780.025 / 0.040
0.450.00330.0001
0.700.00840.0087

Two structural causes, and neither is a tuning error. barGlass is itself a deliberate near-neutral — mixG(fieldTop, navPlane, 0.35), a step between the card and the page — so the base the tint acts on is already below the page's chroma. And the Oklab (a,b) vector mix can cancel rather than add when the page's hue and the accent's differ, which is why several faces measure negative.

So clause 4's target and the contract's own instruction "do not increase opacity first" cannot both hold. At α 0.70 the dark body is still 4.6× short of its floor.

This is also the answer to the contract's own acid test — "turn the 5dp core off: does the crown still look like the theme's glass?" No, and it cannot be made to, because the fix is not a tint coefficient: it is that the glass body's plane would have to be chromatic rather than neutral, which is a change to barGlass's derivation rather than to its paint.

Why clause 4 cannot be met — it is out of gamut, not out of tune

The section below shows the glass body falling short of its floor. Chasing that, I measured the premise and then solved for what would be needed. Both results are stronger than "needs tuning":

1. barGlass is below the page's chroma on 15 of 20 faces. Its own comment says the bar "carries the theme's hue rather than mixing toward a neutral", but mixG(fieldTop, navPlane, 0.35) mixes two near-neutral planes, and the hue drifts 20–29° from the page on several faces (Arctic light 29.6°, Mint & Coral dark 29.2°, Solar dark 28.1°). The tint is being asked to lift a base that is already at or below its surroundings.

2. The chroma that would be required is outside the sRGB gamut at the bar's lightness — on all 20 faces. From VC = alpha · (C_glass − C_page) at the pane's designed alpha of 0.25:

facepage Cneeded C_glassgamut max at that lightnessreachable
ocean light0.01240.11240.0152no
ocean dark0.02200.18200.0436no
mintcoral light0.01990.11990.0080no
system dark0.00820.16820.0834no

The bar sits at the page's lightness — near-white on paper, near-black at night — and those are exactly the two lightnesses where sRGB holds almost no chroma. Raising the alpha cannot fix it either: with the glass plane's chroma gamut-capped, alpha · (C_glass − C_page) is bounded at ~0.003 even at alpha 1.0.

So the only route to clause 4 is to move the bar's lightness off the page's — a mid-tone on paper, a mid-dark at night — where the gamut opens. And even then alpha 0.25 caps the lift at 0.025, so the dark floor of 0.040 additionally needs alpha ≈ 0.45.

That is a real design change, not a constant: the crown would stop being a tint at the page's lightness and become a distinctly placed chromatic band. It is exactly the "coloured glass" the contract asks for, and it is a decision rather than a measurement — so I have not made it unilaterally.

Where the crown's colour actually comes from

The core, and it is not close. Core alpha efficiency 0.61–0.68 and visible salience 0.085–0.440; the body's alpha efficiency is 0.00–0.07. The crown reads as a theme frame because of a 5dp band, and that is worth knowing before anyone tunes the tint further.

Visible chrome — measured after the glass

The previous chrome gates were measuring the wrong quantity

Everything in the section above evaluates the source token. The reader sees the composite:

Cfinal = FAGSL( α·Cchrome + (1−α)·Cunderlay )

A saturated accent behind 0.25 alpha of glass has excellent source chroma and almost none on screen. Measured, the crown's glass body carries a visible salience of 0.003–0.013 against a floor of 0.08–0.10, and an alpha efficiency of 0.00–0.07 — so 93–100% of the signal is being lost in the compositing. The palettes were never the problem, which is exactly what the source-side gates could not see.

The two repairs, and neither one touched the palette

A chromatic core. The crown is no longer uniformly glassy: a 5dp band at its foot carries primaryAccent at 0.62 alpha. That takes the visible salience from 0.003–0.013 to 0.084–0.440 and the alpha efficiency to 0.61–0.67. Every face's core now clears its floor.

The right role for the nav. The active pill was filled with the destination accent — accentProgress for Home — which is the AA-fitted text form, deliberately pushed toward the ink to clear 4.5:1 as foreground type. Used as a fill it produced a pill at 0.03–0.16 Oklab chroma. navigationSelected, the palette's authored chrome accent, carries 1.0–2.7× that. Switching the fill took the nav's visible lift from 0.020–0.036 to 0.060–0.120 and lifted the pass rate from 2/9 to 7/9.

Both repairs are role and compositing changes. Not one palette value moved.

The two remaining failures, and they are marginal rather than systematic

Forest fails the scale-robustness clause: its downsampled crown-core VS is 0.074 against a 0.080 floor. Its light core VS is already the lowest of any face at 0.084, so a third-scale reduction pushes it under. Forest's page is a green-cream and its signature is a gold, which is genuinely the smallest separation in the set.

Moonstone fails the cross-mode clause at a ratio of 0.87 against 0.90. Its dark accent (0xFFFAB2C4, chroma 0.087) is simply less chromatic than its light one (0xFFC9A34D, 0.113), so the dark crown's visible lift cannot reach 90% of the light's. That is a palette observation the rendered gate surfaced — the first one in this whole pass that genuinely is about colour.

Two clauses the shipped design disagrees with — and the app is right to

§4's plane ordering is inverted on every light face. The spec states L(B0) < L(B1) < L(S0) < L(S1). On all nine light faces the app puts backgroundSecondary below backgroundBase, because it uses that role as surfaceVariant — a recess. The spec's clause and the app's usage disagree about what B1 is for; the measurement is reported rather than a theme failed.

§5's chart guide does not match a deuteranope-safe series. The spec asks for a ramp with adjacent steps ≤ 90°. The app's chartSeries is categorical on purpose: its own comment records that it is ordered so no red sits directly beside a green, "the one pairing deuteranopes cannot separate". Five of its seven steps exceed the guide, and every one of them is that ordering doing its job. §15 lists a categorical chart as a failure "without semantic reason" — this one has a reason, and it is written down in the source.

What does hold

§4's planes in band: 52 of 80. Of the 28 out, four are the system pair, which the spec says is not on the sheet; six are chroma below the floor on paper cards, which is the app deliberately stripping hue from a near-white plane; and the rest are within 0.012 of a band edge. The light pages land at L 0.938–0.981 against a 0.94–0.99 band, so terracotta and jade miss by 0.002.

All eight Class-P families pass every gate, Nebula passes its Class-X contract, and the six-family regression set holds. The audit measures dH(primaryAccent, warmAccent) = 4.55° on Nebula's dark face, which is the spec's own recorded invariant to two decimal places.

Two things this render still does not do

The lamp is missing. folioLamp is anchored to whichever cover the screen is featuring, and a screen with no real book behind it has no lamp. On the dark faces that is most of the difference between this and a device: the bare field reads (13,9,26) here against (31,15,35) on the Dusk screenshot.

The blur is the browser's, not Haze. The backdrop blur under each pane is backdrop-filter: blur(20px) — the same radius FolioTokens.blurRadius carries, and the same operation — but it is not the Haze pass, so the progressive fade and the noise floor the app applies are not reproduced.

What the reconstruction found

The plate is far fainter than its ceiling implies

GUILLOCHE_ALPHA_MAX is 0.48 and its own doc measures the plate as being "within ~10% of the brightest it may be". But cover is applied twice: once as the colour mix inside line = mix(field, glow, cover*darkLift), and again as the layer's alpha. Composited, the plate's actual contribution is cover² × intensity — roughly 5% of the glow at a full core on a dark face, and ~2.6% on paper. The geometry is unmistakably there (all nine families are distinct in the sheet), but it is a whisper, not the confident web the constant's calibration describes.

This is a render of what ships, not a judgement about it — but the gap between the documented ceiling and the drawn result is real and worth a decision before anything else is built on top of the plate.

Three semantic anchors have migrated

S asks whether a family's dominant dark chromatic axis is still inside its semantic band. Ocean reads 223° against a 150–210° teal band (13° out, S 61 — passes, barely), solar 343° against 350–70° and jade 137° against 140–205°. Solar and jade are 3–7° outside, which is band-edge noise rather than drift; ocean is the one worth looking at.

What validated the extraction

The spec's section 7 records one frozen relational fact — dH(primaryAccent, warmAccent) ≈ 4.55° on Nebula's dark face. The audit measures 4.55° from the shipped Dusk palette. That is an independent confirmation that the palette extraction and the Oklab conversion both agree with the state the spec was written from.

Two spec sections are superseded, and one is not implementable as written

  • Section 13 (geometry) describes cubic Bézier ribbons with a monotone seam splitter. The shipped shader is not that: it is three crossed sine waves whose interference is the ribbon. The renders use the shader. Reconstructing the Bézier description would produce an image the app does not draw.
  • Section 14 (luminosity) asks bright filaments to follow local curvature, alpha_i = a0*(1 + 0.9|kappa_i|/kappa_max). The shipped waveLine has no curvature term; brightness is the family warp and the tier share. Not implemented.
  • Section 7 (the Nebula contract) states its own frozen literal tolerances did not survive and instructs a versioned reconstruction. The contract here is nebula-x/v1-reconstructed, seeded from the surviving role/hue facts, and it reports tolerances_recovered: false rather than pretending otherwise.

Reproducing this

  • python extract.py — reads FolioArtDirection.kt, GuillocheShader.android.kt, AmbientShader.android.kt, GuillocheModel.kt and FolioLight.kt; writes faces.json and agsl.json. Nothing is retyped.
  • python build.py — builds the WebGL page and renders all twenty faces through headless Chrome. The AGSL source is type-renamed and its main moved one level down so the body stays verbatim; no expression is rewritten.
  • python audit.py — the canonical identity metrics and the regression assertions.
  • python benchmarks.py — the spec's §4, §11, §15 and §17 clauses as assertions.
  • python sheet.py — the face contact sheet.
  • python screen.py — the whole screen: the ground plane plus every pane of glass, laid out to FolioTokens.
  • python screen_sheet.py — the Home contact sheet.
  • python report.py — this page.

What is not drawn here

The render is the ground plane: the field, the plate and the ambient film. It is not the whole screen. Missing, in layer order: folioLamp (one light source anchored to the featured book cover — there is no cover in a bare field render), and everything above it: the masthead, the content, and the navigation capsule. Sampling the bare field in a real device screenshot of the Dusk face gives (31,15,35) where this render gives (13,9,26); the gap is the lamp. Closing it needs a featured cover, which is a screen-level input rather than a ground-plane one.
